title: Scoring sourdough, the single-slash ear
subtitle: How to cut the loaf before baking so it opens where you intend
excerpt: Scoring the surface of sourdough before it goes into the oven controls where the crust splits. A single confident slash at a shallow angle produces the raised, crisp ear that characterises a well-baked country loaf. Depth and angle matter more than speed.
sourceNotes: Bread scoring technique draws on standard sourdough baking practice. The 30 to 45 degree angle for producing an ear is a widely accepted guideline for country loaves.

recipe.yieldDescription: Technique applied to any shaped sourdough loaf

glossaryTerms.definition: The raised flap of crust that lifts along a score line during baking. An ear indicates good surface tension, a well-proofed loaf, and a shallow scoring angle.

The rapid rise that happens in the first 10 to 15 minutes of baking as steam from the crust and the heat expand the gas pockets in the dough. Scoring allows oven spring to be directed outward through the cut rather than bursting randomly.

content.text: somewhere to go. Without a score, the pressure of rising gas finds its own weak point and blows out unpredictably. A clean score at the right angle produces the raised, curling
that is a sign of a well-baked sourdough.

A bread knife or any razor-sharp blade works. A lame (a baking razor on a handle) gives more control on high-hydration doughs. Whatever you use, it must be sharp; a blunt blade drags the surface and deflates the loaf instead of cutting cleanly.
Remove the shaped loaf from the fridge. It should be firm and cold, much easier to score than a room-temperature loaf.
Hold the blade at a 30 to 45 degree angle relative to the surface of the loaf, not perpendicular to it. A shallow angle is what produces the ear.
Make one confident cut from one end of the loaf to the other in a single motion. Aim for 1 to 1.5 cm depth. Hesitating produces a dragged, ragged cut.
Load the loaf into the hot Dutch oven immediately.

No ear, loaf spreads flat: the score angle was too steep (perpendicular), the loaf was overproofed, or the dough lacked surface tension during shaping. Flat with burst sides: no score, or the score was too shallow and closed up under oven spring.
